Email exchange with Greg and Brett, Brett, to summarize our call and next steps. Also looping in my team.  

PowerShelter builds battery locker and swap systems. Developed in the Netherlands, deployed across the EU and UK, now entering the US and looking for site partners.

The concept: put swap lockers at XoomPark pit stops. E-bikes, scooters and delivery robots pull in, swap a depleted battery for a charged one in under a minute, and go back out. No charging dwell, no trip back to a hub or depot. The vehicle stays inside the demand zone, which is the same thing we sell car fleets, applied to small vehicles.

Why our sites fit: we already have what a locker needs. Space, power, security, and staff on site. The footprint is small and it consumes no stalls, so it sits alongside car staging rather than competing with it.

What it brings us: a new customer segment on infrastructure we're already paying for. Delivery platforms and micromobility fleets (DoorDash, Serve, Coco, Zoomo, Whizz) all have the same problem and none of them need a parking space to solve it. It also puts a product on sites that can't support car charging, which widens what counts as a usable site for us.

Open items: which metros they're prioritizing, footprint and power requirements per unit, who pays for the hardware, and how revenue splits between them and the site. We're active in Phoenix, San Diego, SF, LA, Austin, Dallas and Miami, and our API can be queried for capacity by location.

Next step: three-way call with Carlin at DoorDash, and our teams

Greg Bessoni
CEO, XoomPark

New Austin opening, straight from a Waymo conversation. Two threads:
1. Event PUDO lots — same model as the 49ers operation. Waymo wants dedicated lots positioned just outside the traffic-control perimeter during large events. Their spec:
As close to the venue as possible without being inside the closure zone
Pickup timed and paired with the rider — car and rider arrive together, no dwell
Walk of 3 blocks or less, stretchable for a big event
Fast egress — out of event traffic and moving toward the destination quickly

They asked us: which lots can run PUDO, capacity at each, and what infrastructure is on site. The two screens that decide everything: proximity to the venue and a clean path out.

We're in good shape. Start conversations again with the BID and City (both of which we've spoken with but now have more traction I believe)

2. @Bern Grush — live lead for CurbReserver. The same Waymo contact cares a lot about geofence management for emergency and construction situations — they want it managed, not improvised. Squarely your wheelhouse; happy to make the intro this week.

As promised, attached is the rate card. It includes three billing structures, each with ranges and the key drivers so you can position any site appropriately.

The second tab features a site estimator. By entering the vehicle count, stall count, charger type, coverage hours, and fleet type, it will generate an estimated monthly range across all three models. Please note this is intended as a working tool rather than a final quote.

One important detail to highlight: charger type and quantity are very important variables in the per-vehicle structure. L2 overnight sites and L3 fast-charge sites operate on significantly different session cadences and more touchpoints, which impacts the monthly rate. Of the three options, the per-task and per-vehicle structures will translate most directly into how you price services for your fleets. The hourly structure is included primarily as a benchmark.

Greg,

Appreciate you laying this out, and I understand your position. The straight answer: we don't grant exclusivity, radius restrictions, or referral locks to anyone, at any size. We hold this line with the largest operators in the space, even the public companies we work with who contract for 3-years at high volume, so it's a firm-wide position rather than a judgment on XoomPark.
